articles.title: Why India has soured on Trump ahead of US midterms
articles.summary: Seven years after Modi backed Trump, New Delhi may now hope US midterm losses leave the president chastened.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India — Standing next to United States President Donald Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivered praise after praise.

“Every time [we meet], he has been the same: warm, friendly, accessible, energetic, and full of wit,” he said of Trump, as they addressed a joint rally in a Houston, Texas, stadium packed with more than 50,000 Indian Americans.

That was in 2019, ahead of the 2020 US presidential vote, when Trump was facing a major electoral test – seeking re-election to a second term. Modi was, in effect, galvanising support for him among the Indian-American community, the wealthiest diaspora in the US.

Modi even borrowed a line from his own successful election campaigns, saying: “Abki baar, Trump sarkaar!”, Hindi for “This time, a Trump government.”

Seven years later, as Trump prepares for difficult midterm elections that could see him lose significant numbers in the US Congress, potentially crippling his legislative agenda, New Delhi’s equation with Washington could not be more different.

Far from endorsing Trump, Indian officials have in recent weeks been more direct than ever in their criticism of his administration, amid a series of setbacks to bilateral ties. And many analysts believe the Modi government may now actually prefer a Trump chastened by midterm losses.

India has long enjoyed bipartisan support in Washington. Yet traditionally, New Delhi’s strategic community has often felt more comfortable with Republican presidents in power.

It was under Ronald Reagan, as the Cold War wound down, that India and the US reset ties after decades of mistrust amid New Delhi’s strong relationship with Moscow. Then, between 2006 and 2008, under George W Bush, India and the US struck a landmark civil nuclear deal. India was allowed access to global nuclear technology and fuel despite not being a signatory to the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). Under Bush, India and the US also signed major military pacts, including allowing US ships and planes refuelling and logistical access to Indian bases.

By contrast, New Delhi has often seen US Democratic administrations as more critical of India’s human rights record.

The tradition of friendly ties with US Republican presidents appeared set to continue under Trump, amid visible bonhomie between the US leader and Modi. The Indian prime minister even called Trump “India’s best friend in the White House”.

But Trump 2.0 has been very different, from India’s perspective.

So different that New Delhi has chosen to break with a long-held practice. India usually addresses divisive issues with friendly nations quietly, behind the scenes. But months of tensions on a string of issues have pushed India to adopt a more openly critical tone towards the White House.

Last month, speaking at an event in New York, India’s foreign minister, Minister of External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, shared a pointed, blunt assessment of the Trump administration: It has been an insensitive partner to India’s concerns over “terrorism”; has warmed to its archrival Pakistan; and has pursued “self-centred” trade policies that have disproportionately hurt the Global South.

“Countries should not be so self-centred that you’re in your own world and take your decision, and say, ‘Well, it was not my intention to make your life difficult’,” he said.

One of the biggest sticking points between both capitals is an elusive trade deal that could bring relief to India, among the worst-hit countries under Trump’s tariff regime.

Earlier this month, India’s finance minister, Minister of Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman, said that the negotiations had reached a “plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very difficult”.

Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement has also often targeted Indians and Indian Americans, using racist tropes, accusing them of “stealing” jobs in the United States via programmes like the H-1B visa schemes. Anti-Indian rhetoric on US social media is at an all-time high. And early in his second term, Trump sent many undocumented Indian immigrants back home shackled in chains – a visual that stirred outrage in India.

Milan Vaishnav, director of the South Asia programme at the Washington, DC-based Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think tank, said the Indian government “can tolerate genuine policy differences with a US administration”. However, “the attacks on India and Indian Americans coming from this administration, and many of their allies in the media and on social media, have struck a nerve,” he said.

Vaishnav, like other analysts, told Al Jazeera that despite recent criticism coming from New Delhi, “the Modi government has shown admirable restraint in its response”.

Since Trump returned to office in 2025, the US-India relationship has been beset by a seemingly never-ending series of crises.

Some of the irritants are: punitive US tariffs and stalled trade negotiations; Washington’s pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil; Trump’s repeated claims that he mediated an India-Pakistan ceasefire in 2025, which New Delhi rejects; closer US ties with Pakistan despite India’s concerns over “terrorism”; higher H-1B specialised worker visa fees in the US, and Trump’s wider immigration crackdown affecting Indian workers.

At one point, India was among the countries facing the worst Trump-imposed tariff rates. After the US Supreme Court in February struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs on numerous nations, his administration swiftly turned to other tools, including a new 10 percent global tariff.

Last month, Trump signed a law under which the US can impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries like India that buy Russian oil. However, he paused it to avoid driving up energy prices in the US ahead of November’s midterm elections, while keeping negotiations with Russia over Moscow’s war in Ukraine on track.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited India’s financial hub Mumbai this week, but skipped the capital, said in an interview with The Indian Express that “none of these tariffs are meant to punish or harm India”.

Rubio argued that Washington’s “broader foreign policy, unfortunately, involves a war going on between Russia and Ukraine” — and added that “one of the reasons why [Trump paused the tariff] is because he understands that it would have a very detrimental impact on a very important relationship with India”.

But Rubio did not rule out that similar measures would return in a matter of time. “I think the president is trying very hard to balance that… but it will be a challenge”, he remarked.

Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera: “Under Trump 2.0, the bipartisan consensus on India seems to have ended in Washington.

“The sentiment [in Washington] seems too strong to be attributed solely to President Trump; it points to the broader American establishment,” Donthi said.

The measures undertaken by the Trump administration “have brought back distrust of the US among the Indian strategic establishment”, he said, referring to Cold War-era tensions.

The upcoming US midterm elections are crucial for Trump. If he loses control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, it would give Democrats more power to scrutinise his administration’s policies.

Trump is facing the worst approval ratings of his political career amid record-high gas prices in the US due to the global energy crisis triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February this year.

Vaishnav, of Carnegie Endowment, said that “a chastened Trump would be in India’s interests”.

“There are many Democrats on Capitol Hill, not to mention Republicans, who are livid with this administration’s handling of US-India ties,” he said. “While they might have their criticisms of India’s politics, economics, and foreign policy, they genuinely believe in the logic of a strong US-India partnership.”

A Democrat-dominated Congress could have a “moderating impact” on Washington’s foreign policy, he said.

But Michael Kugelman, a Washington-based analyst on South Asia, said he doubts Trump’s foreign policy would be affected by the election results, “at least not when it comes to the question of India”.

Kugelman noted that Trump is entering the last era of his presidency – he cannot legally run for a third term – and “he is going to continue to pursue a policy that he would think could best advance US economic interests” when it comes to dealing with New Delhi.

“If he thinks that could entail threatening additional tariffs on India, then he would do that.”

Crisis Group’s Donthi told Al Jazeera that New Delhi would hope that bilateral relations improve after Trump leaves office, “and that [Washington] can take a more patient, strategic approach”.

But, meanwhile, he said, a weakened Trump might not necessarily bring relief to India, “as there seems to be broader consensus [among Trump-aligned Republicans] on the need to pressure India”.

For New Delhi, that landscape marks a dramatic shift from just a few years ago.

Two years back, days after Trump had won the 2024 election, Foreign Minister Jaishankar said, with a wide smile, that “many countries are nervous about the US today, but let’s be honest — we [India] are not one of them”.

articles.title: RFK Jr. faces widespread rebuke over his anti-Arab remarks
articles.summary: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. faced widespread rebuke Tuesday over anti-Arab comments that the Council on American-Islamic Relations cast as “a textbook display of unvarnished racism and bigotry.”
articles.body: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. faced widespread rebuke from civil rights groups, health care advocates and Democrats on Tuesday over anti-Arab comments that the Council on American-Islamic Relations cast as “a textbook display of unvarnished racism and bigotry.” In his remarks Monday at a campaign event in Michigan where Republican Mike Rogers is running for the U.S. Senate against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, Kennedy falsely claimed that Arabs had not won major international awards and “don’t produce” science and literature. “There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce literature,” he said. Arabs have won all those prizes. Peter Hotez, who is a professor at the Baylor College of Medicine and specializes in vaccine development and tropical medicine, said his late colleague, Nobel Prize winner Ahmed Zewail, who was Arab and died in 2016, “would disagree” with Kennedy’s comments. The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment. U.S. rights advocates have raised concerns over escalating rhetoric against Muslims, Arabs, immigrants and ethnic minorities by President Donald Trump and his allies during the ongoing midterm election campaign. “Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s vile anti-Arab rant is a textbook display of unvarnished racism and bigotry,” the Council on American-Islamic Relations, which documents hate against Muslims and Arabs in the U.S., said Tuesday. “His sweeping erasure of Arab contributions to humanity is not only maliciously false, but it also fans the flames of anti-Arab and anti-Muslim hate at a time when communities are already vulnerable to bigoted attacks from other public officials nationwide.” Kennedy said the rise of the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world’s oldest and most influential Islamist groups founded almost a century ago, had “created stagnant societies.” Republicans have claimed, without evidence, that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood even as the Democrat has publicly disavowed the group and denied any connection to it. El-Sayed, a medical doctor and former public health official who would be the first Muslim U.S. senator if elected, has faced a host of anti-Muslim attacks during the campaign. Over the weekend, Trump invoked the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks when speaking about El-Sayed, whom he has also repeatedly and falsely called a “jihadist.” A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign on Tuesday accused Kennedy of making racially charged comments in an attempt to influence voters. “It’s rich to have an anti-scientist come to Michigan to lecture a doctor with two doctoral degrees who has spent his entire career working on public health,” said Cole Wozniak, the spokesperson. Senator Chris Murphy, D-Conn., also criticized Kennedy’s comments. “I really think everyone needs to pay attention to this coordinated campaign to delegitimize Muslim Americans — not just as citizens but as humans,” he said in a post on X. The U.S. health care advocacy organization and nonprofit Protect Our Care cast Kennedy’s comments as a “wildly racist tirade.” Kennedy, who has pushed his anti-vaccine views in his role as the top health official, was also in Michigan on Monday to promote funding for Detroit’s health department and touted agreements with hospitals to offer healthier food.

articles.title: Netanyahu outlines achievements, future plans as Likud leads Israeli polls
articles.summary: Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says ‘true’ election results due in one or two days.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that a right-wing government must be formed to ensure Israel’s long-term security, and that it cannot rely on coalitions with Arab parties “that are against our existence”.

He made the comments to supporters at his Likud party headquarters in West Jerusalem on Tuesday, several hours after polls closed in Israel’s legislative election and the early results were being announced.

With more than half of ballots counted , The Times of Israel projected Netanyahu’s bloc to win 56 seats and Gadi Eisenkot’s alliance, 49.

Neither is likely to secure a clear path to a governing majority.

Netanyahu said the “true results” were still one or two days away, while acknowledging that Likud was projected to become the “largest party in Israel”.

Likud was on track to win an estimated 27 seats to 21 for Eisenkot’s Yashar party, according to projections from Israeli Channels 12 and 13, giving Likud a clear lead over all others in the parliament.

Netanyahu also highlighted his achievements since taking office in his current term from 2022, which he sought to build upon.

“We worked wonders that changed the face of the Middle East. We eliminated [Mohammed] Deif, [Ismail] Haniyeh, [Yahya] Sinwar, [Hassan] Nasrallah, [Iranian Supreme Leader Ali] Khamenei,” he said.

“We established security zones deep inside Gaza, in Lebanon, in Syria. We removed an immediate existential threat that hung over us, the danger of immediate destruction. We struck the Iranian regime and brought it to the edge of the abyss. Iran is weaker than ever; Israel is stronger than ever.”

He said Israel had a “historical opportunity” together with United States President Donald Trump “to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all”.

Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador who served as consul general of Israel in New York City, said the party that secures the majority of seats may have to seek an uncomfortable coalition deal in order to govern.

But he said opposition voters would not want the bloc to strike a deal with Netanyahu’s coalition.

Marwan Bishara, Al Jazeera’s senior political analyst, says Netanyahu attempted to put on a “brave face” about his party’s prospects during his speech in Jerusalem.

“It’s clear that he’s trying also to project a kind of success that he doesn’t merit. One, because he cannot form a coalition, but two, the idea that he is the largest party in Israel kind of hides the fact that this is the lowest Likud has reached since 2009.”

Political analyst Dan Perry told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu used his speech to “spin the situation as best as he could” after exit polls were released.

articles.title: Sheffield music 'really healthy', says Cabaret Voltaire veteran
articles.summary: The band, pioneers of electronic and industrial music in the 1970s and 80s, says farewell.
articles.body:
The future of Sheffield music looks "really healthy", one of Cabaret Voltaire's founding members has said after winding up the band's 50-year career in the city.

Chris Watson joined fellow founder Stephen Mallinder at the city's Octagon Centre on Sunday night to complete their UK-wide tour and finish where they had started in the mid-1970s.

The sold-out homecoming marks the end of a band that was at the forefront of a revolution in popular music, which saw musicians turn away from guitars towards wire-sprouting modular synthesisers and bedroom laptops.

Speaking to the BBC after the show, Watson said there was "a really good atmosphere" at the Octagon with "a lot of love in the room".

About finishing in Sheffield, he said: "It was perfect. I mean, we started there 50 years ago so that's the place we were always going to finish it and that's our, for Mal and I, the two remaining members, that's our home city so we were certain that's where we wanted to close the chapter."

The third founding member, Richard H Kirk, died in 2021.

Sheffield music journalist Daniel Dylan Wray, who was at the final show, said the band's influence had been "incalculable".

"They were originators and pioneers, doing it years ahead of everyone else, and blazing a trail that many others would follow," he said.

"The world of electronic, dance, industrial and post-punk music as we know it today was shaped by their output – everything from Detroit techno to groups like Nine Inch Nails via Sheffield's own rich lineage of electronic music, has all been touched and moulded by their greatness."

Cabaret Voltaire took their name from the Zurich club that became the birthplace of the Dadaist art movement in 1916.

German artist Hugo Ball, who travelled to Switzerland amid the horrors of World War One, teamed up with other emigres to perform anarchic, prank-like shows.

Its influence spread across Western artistic styles throughout the 20th Century and its rambunctious energy was adopted by artists looking to cause chaos and flip entrenched assumptions of what art should be.

For the Sheffield trio, whose early experiments sound akin to a sentient synthesiser having a nightmare, the Dadaists were an open door towards a performance style which some audiences found difficult to accept.

At one of their first shows, which Watson said the band had "blagged" at the University of Sheffield's students' union, they "confronted" an audience who were expecting disco.

He said the students were "ironically, people who you would think are front-thinking, people who would be interested in something new, and of course they weren't".

The musician added: "They were outraged by something that they couldn't think they could dance to, and so it just descended into this beautiful chaos, which we were really proud of."

Sonically, Watson drew on Sheffield's soundscapes, and he was also inspired by musique concréte, an art form that developed in France in the 1940s as a way of turning raw environmental sounds into musical compositions.

This led him to a career in producing sound for BBC radio and wildlife documentaries with Sir David Attenborough after he left the band in 1981.

He described the final Cabaret Voltaire tour as a celebration, rather than a reunion, because of Kirk's absence.

Nick Potter, a music programme producer at the University of Sheffield, said: "'It was a real honour to be able to host Cabaret Voltaire for their final ever gig - metres away from where they played their first in the students' union's Upper Refectory.

"Cabaret Voltaire have a long history here - including filming music videos in the drama studio and Chris Watson's honorary doctorate.

"Their legacy of innovation and experimentation is a real point of pride for the city, and Sunday's gig was a perfect way to finish everything off."

Wray said the show at the Octagon, which holds up to 1,800 people, brought people from all over the world and of all ages.

He described the show as "a little bit of history" and "one of those gigs that felt like a privilege to be there for and witness".

When asked why he believed Sheffield's musical future to be healthy, Watson said: "Because it's driven by young people, people with fresh, inquiring, intelligent minds, who aren't just seeking 15 minutes of fame on social media but are interested in making music that has its own life and genre and depth and integrity to it.

"That's the kind of music that I enjoy listening to."

articles.title: Knowsley Halloween costume swap helps families save money
articles.summary: One mother said Halloween outfits are "completely extortionate" as families pick up free alternatives.
articles.body:
Parents in Merseyside are turning to a free Halloween costume swap scheme to avoid prices one mother described as "completely extortionate".

Lola Roberts, who visited Prescot Library with her children, said her son had chosen a clown costume costing £40, so she showed him free alternatives.

Knowsley Council is running the scheme during half-term to help families save money and reduce the number of costumes thrown away after Halloween.

Organisers said the scheme had proved popular, with children trying on costumes and taking part in craft activities.

Roberts said she had originally visited the library after seeing a poster advertising an activity where children could decorate their own bags.

After discovering the swap shop, she said she was pleased to see so many families taking part.

She said she had already put aside a bag of unwanted costumes at home and welcomed the opportunity for other families to reuse them.

"There's such a good sense of community here," she said.

Roberts called for similar events to be held throughout the year, saying children also needed fancy dress outfits for school discos and other occasions.

She said she did not want children to feel left out because their families could not afford costumes.

Grace Barlow, from Knowsley Council's recycling engagement team, said the initiative aimed to ease financial pressure on parents while reducing textile waste.

"There's such a huge pressure on parents to be buying new costumes every year," she said.

Barlow, who has two children, said she knew how costumes could end up being stored away or thrown out after only one use.

She said the council had previously held popular events offering pre-loved Christmas jumpers and hoped the Halloween scheme would continue in future years.

The council is encouraging families to donate unwanted costumes at collection points in its libraries after Halloween so they can be reused next year.

articles.title: Hampshire Free haircuts project aims to inspire other stylists
articles.summary: Georgia Chappels runs free community haircuts to help those feeling the impact of rising costs.
articles.body:
A hair stylist from Ringwood is hoping to inspire other hairdressers across the country to offer free haircuts.

A few years ago, Georgia Chappels found herself in a 'financial crisis' after going through a divorce. She relied on foodbanks and charities to support her family.

Now she runs the Community Haircuts project in Hampshire - offering a free, drop-in service with no questions asked.

She says: "I can't give back monetary value into the community, but I can give back my time."

Chappels and other stylists from the area have run the project for a year, from several venues across Hampshire and Dorset.

She hopes that it will help anyone struggling while the cost of living continues to rise.

"People are making ends meet", she said.

"The mum might work two jobs, the dad works full time. Yes, they've got a mortgage. Yes, they've got a car.

"But the bills and everything after everything's gone - there's no money for luxuries such as a haircut."

And it isn't just for parents and their children - the service is for everyone and has been used by students and elderly members of the community too.

Barber Thomas Perriman only recently started his career but has decided to give up some of his time to help out.

He said: "It's so important to give back when you've maybe gone through stuff yourself.

"Everyone in the community deserves to get their hair cut in an environment which, for whatever reason, they might not be able to get to normally."

Likewise, Chappels still works in a salon four days a week, alongside the Community Haircut events held regularly.

While they do not have the same facilities or products that may be used in a salon, the team aims to make it feel as luxury as possible.

Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight

Events are advertised on their Facebook page and Chappels hopes to spread the word so other hair stylists offer their time to offer a similar service.

"I would love to inspire other hairdressers up and down the country to maybe roll it out in their local community. It takes a couple of hours a month.

"The difference a haircut can make is it makes you feel like you again. It's more than just a haircut."

articles.title: Work to turn derelict courthouse into Wiltshire Museum begins
articles.summary: The listed building in Devizes is expected to reopen in 2030 as the new home of Wiltshire Museum.
articles.body:
The £14.5m transformation of a derelict courthouse building into the new home of a county museum has begun.

The Grade II* listed Assize Court in Devizes, Wiltshire, was built in 1835 and has been unused since it closed in the 1980s.

It is expected to reopen in 2030 as the new home of Wiltshire Museum - which is currently based in a smaller building in the town and has a number of collections, including gold items found in burial sites near Stonehenge.

The preliminary works will last for about 12 weeks and prepare the historic building ahead of the main works which are due to start early next year. Assizes for Devizes Programme Manager Nicola Trowell said it was a "monumental" first step.

Wiltshire Museum was granted planning permission by Wiltshire Council to restore the historic court in August 2025.

As well as exhibition space, the new museum site will have a cafe, learning space, multi-use event space and gardens. The current site - which is not large enough to hold all of the museum's collections - is set to become a collections discovery centre.

Devizes Town Mayor Vanessa Tanner said: "Having the Wiltshire Museum in Devizes is such a great opportunity for the people in our town, our county and tourists from all over the world."

"I'm really excited to see the historic Assizes Court brought back to life thanks to the vision and tireless efforts of the Museum team, the National Lottery Fund and all those people who have generously donated their time and money to make it happen," she added.

The initial works involve the removal of lead paint, lime plaster and ceiling, as part of efforts to conserve the listed building.

Trowell said: "The start of the enabling works is a monumental - and first truly visible - step in our project to save the Assize Court and transform it into a new home for the Wiltshire Museum."

The project received £8.5m of funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund in December 2025.

More than £12.5m has been raised so far to finance the project with additional support from individuals, trusts and foundations. Museum director David Dawson previously told the BBC he was confident the gap in funds would be closed by ongoing grant bids.

articles.title: Maryland removed its Cypress Mill dam in 2025; officials report more than 35 miles of fish habitat reopened, while early plans estimated 18 miles
articles.summary: The removal of Maryland's Cypress Mill Dam, built around 1900, has restored 35 miles of vital habitat for herring, shad, and other migratory fish species, marking a significant environmental restoration effort in the Chesapeake Bay region.
articles.body: Dams built to power mills can continue to obstruct migratory fish long after their original purpose has ended. One such structure stood near Millington on Maryland's Eastern Shore, where Cypress Branch Dam was removed in 2025 after decades of deterioration and planning. Although the dam had breached years earlier, the remaining structure continued to impede fish passage.The structure, called Cypress Branch Dam in state records and also known as Cypress Mill Dam, was built to hold water for the mill races in Millington. Its exact construction date is unknown, but consultants estimated that it dated to about 1900 based on the aggregate in the concrete. The Maryland Department of Natural Resources reports that removal was completed in April 2025, reopening more than 35 miles of habitat for herring, hickory shad and other fish. The project required years of planning, several rounds of funding and work to resolve a railway crossing issue.A dam from the mill eraThe dam consisted of an earthen berm and a concrete spillway. It had breached decades before its removal and was in an advanced state of disrepair, but the remaining structure still obstructed fish passage. A large mill pond to the north fed a smaller pond to the south, which supplied the mill races in Millington.No one knows exactly when it was built. The state’s history of the site says there have been dams and mill ponds in the area since the 18th century. Consultants from Hurt and Proffitt estimated the current dam dated to about 1900, based on the aggregate in the concrete. The estate passed through a lengthy line of owners, including Philadelphia merchant Thomas Gilpin in the 1760s and subsequently the Higman family, whose grist mill gave the property one of its names. The mill pond property was purchased by the state of Maryland in 1994. It is currently part of Cypress Branch State Park.Taking it downAmerican Rivers, which worked with the state on the restoration, said the history is a remnant of the Eastern Shore’s milling era with no recognised builder. Work started in 2019 when the Maryland Geological Survey tested the silt behind the dam and discovered it wasn’t toxic and the amounts were low because the dam had been ruptured for so long, American Rivers said.The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service was an early booster, seeing an opportunity to reunite more than 35 miles of habitat. Then the pandemic slowed the design work. Construction expenses went up. And the project required more money. That came in the form of a grant from the Environmental Protection Agency, through the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. Permits took time, too, in part because the site needed historical mitigation and a strategy for what to do if the restoration didn’t work out the way they hoped.Construction began in early 2025. Crews demolished the concrete of the old spillway, relocated parts of the earthen dam and straightened out a canal that had broken up into multiple pieces to go around the spillway. They also built big structures of root wad along the banks to hold the soil in place. A late issue was a railway crossing near the access road, which was rectified on the way out thanks to a state financial increase.What the river gets backThe target species include alewife and blueback herring, collectively known as river herring, and hickory shad. These fish spend their adult lives in the Atlantic and return to freshwater each spring to spawn. An early Maryland Department of Natural Resources planning document estimated that the project would reconnect 18 miles of habitat, comprising more than eight miles of Cypress Branch and 10 miles of tributaries. After completion, the department reported that the project reopened more than 35 miles of habitat. The two figures come from different stages of the project, and the published documents do not explain exactly how the latter total was calculated.The project forms part of a wider effort to restore migratory fish routes throughout the Chesapeake Bay watershed. The Chesapeake Bay Program originally set a goal of opening 1,000 additional stream miles to fish passage by 2025. Partners achieved that target in 2016, nine years ahead of schedule. Under a later goal, partners opened 303 stream miles during 2022 and 2023. These are separate milestones, so the later figures do not conflict with the earlier achievement. The Cypress Branch project team also established a monitoring plan to assess whether herring and shad return in healthy numbers. After the restoration work, American Rivers documented an osprey catching a fish in the former pond area. The Cypress Branch project shows that a breached, disused dam can continue to impede fish migration long after its original purpose has disappeared. articles.title: The next phase of military rule in Egypt is here
articles.summary: El-Sisi’s announcement that he will not run for a fourth term may signal a new leadership arrangement.
articles.body:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi surprised observers when he recently announced his intention to leave office after his third presidential term ends in April 2030.

El-Sisi had been widely suspected of moving to amend the Egyptian constitution to allow him to serve another term, or possibly indefinitely.

But speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy, el-Sisi insisted that his departure was a settled matter and that “no one would tamper with” the constitution.

So what is behind the decision? There has been much speculation that el-Sisi may use this declaration to rally popular support for a fourth term or preempt a move by the military against him. But there is also the possibility that he is setting up the next phase of military rule in Egypt.

It is important to point out first that voluntarily leaving power is a risky proposition for any authoritarian leader.

In el-Sisi’s case, his 2030 departure would leave open the possibility that a future Egyptian government could seek to use him as a scapegoat for the country’s problems, possibly even holding him to account for alleged crimes committed during his presidency.

El-Sisi led a coup in 2013 against Egypt’s first democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, which was accompanied by massacres and the jailing of tens of thousands of politicians, activists, and journalists.

El-Sisi’s economic record has also been the subject of criticism, with detractors accusing him and his government of corruption , poor fiscal policy and lavish spending on vanity projects. Egypt’s debt stands at 81 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), with interest payments alone exceeding combined spending on healthcare, education, wages and subsidies. Meanwhile, the Egyptian pound has lost more than 80 percent of its value against the US dollar since 2014, while cumulative inflation exceeds 460 percent.

In this context, el-Sisi’s announcement that he plans to step down in 2030 was rather unexpected. Some have speculated that he has no intention of actually leaving office and could go back on his statement, as he has done before.

In 2013, following Morsi’s overthrow, el-Sisi denied that he would run for president.

After telling the media in 2017 that he was committed to “preserving [the constitution’s] two four-year terms and not changing it”, he helped lead the drive to amend the constitution in 2019.

A judicial source told Mada Masr last week that el-Sisi’s announcement left open the door for a “popular call” for the president to remain in office.

A second possibility is that with this move, el-Sisi may be attempting to preempt a possible military intervention, which could become more likely if the economy continues to falter.

In 2011, the military responded to popular protests against former President Hosni Mubarak by forcing him to step down.

The army could attempt to defuse public anger by presenting el-Sisi as a scapegoat, forcibly removing him from power, and replacing him with someone who can preserve a measure of stability as well as secure its vast economic interests.

In that context, a member of parliament said recently that he has heard el-Sisi say in private meetings that he would rather step down than wait for the military to force him out.

But a third and much more likely possibility deserves particular attention: el-Sisi may be preparing to leave the presidency while ensuring that Egypt’s military-dominated political system survives his departure.

It is perhaps not coincidental that during the announcement, he cited Article 200 of the constitution, which gives the armed forces an extraordinary role in Egyptian politics.

The article, amended in 2019, makes the military responsible for maintaining the country’s “democracy” and the “gains, rights and freedoms” of the Egyptian people.

According to el-Sisi, the aim of the article is “to protect the Egyptian state from any attempt to infiltrate it or allow people to take it over who cannot handle the responsibility of this country or who do not even understand the meaning of ‘state’”.

Article 200, combined with Article 234 — which requires that a president secure approval from the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces before appointing a defence minister — gives the military significant control over Egyptian political life.

El-Sisi’s vision for the selection of Egypt’s next president gives the military an outsized role. His proposal includes setting up a committee of experts to draft legislation for selecting hundreds of highly educated Egyptians to undergo specialised training at the Egyptian Military Academy.

Applicants, el-Sisi proposes, should hold doctoral degrees, be between 40 and 50 years of age, and be prepared to spend 30 months at the academy learning about the Egyptian state.

The programme would also train future ministers, governors and members of parliament.

Combined with Articles 200 and 234, this proposed mechanism seems intended to preserve the military’s dominance long after el-Sisi leaves office. It could be favourable to him as well.

A genuinely independent, civilian president could seek to investigate massacres overseen by el-Sisi, allegations of corruption, or other alleged crimes. A transition process closely managed by the military is highly unlikely to yield such a result.

The open question now is how an increasingly frustrated and critical Egyptian public will respond to a political process managed by the military that effectively wipes out the need for a popular mandate.

For now, el-Sisi and the military appear determined to shape Egypt’s political future. But the people may have the last word.

articles.title: Mum quit law to voice characters on Netflix show, Spike
articles.summary: Emily McGonagle, 42, decides to change careers after watching Peppa Pig and Paw Patrol on repeat.
articles.body:
A mum says she left her late-night legal career behind for voiceover work from home where she can care for her children.

Emily McGonagle started her working life as a lawyer in the capital, often finishing at 03:00, but started to question whether she could sustain it long term.

After having children, she decided to seek something "more flexible" than her daily commute from Colchester to Canary Wharf, and pivoted to voiceover work in 2019.

The 42-year-old voices eight characters for the children's television series Spike, which premiered on Netflix on 12 October and is its number one children's show on the site in the UK.

The cartoon began as a preschool animation on YouTube called Fire Spike!, which was about the adventures of a dragon and his friends.

It was created by a Lithuanian company called Bored Panda, founded in 2009.

When McGonagle joined the team, it had "less than 1,000 subscribers and minimal views".

It now has 1.25m subscribers and was the seventh most-watched Netflix show globally in its first week.

Is home-working under threat from the perks of office life?

McGonagle's curiosity was stirred while her toddlers were watching television.

She said: "I just kind of always wondered about it, and then I was also watching a lot of kids' TV, like Paw Patrol and Peppa Pig, on repeat.

"I'd be like, 'Oh, that'll be such a cool job. I'd love to do that,' but how on earth do you get into it?'.

"I kind of just wrote it off because I don't have an acting background."

She told BBC Essex how she filled her home studio with professional audio equipment, and after several months of auditioning, got her first gig with Google.

She did commercials, signed up to some acting groups in Colchester and did a six-week acting course in London.

Three years ago she saw the advert for Spike.

"If you'd have asked me, when I was watching Peppa Pig all those years ago with my kids, that I'd be hearing my own voice on radio and Netflix, it would be beyond my wildest expectations."

Ahead of its Netflix debut, Bored Panda group's head of animation, Jonas Dovydaitis, said on social media he could not "get over how cool" that children around the world could now watch the show on the platform.

articles.title: Academics, doctors, actors: How Serbia’s 250-member parliament will look after students-led movement's win
articles.summary: Serbia’s Aleksandar Vučić has conceded defeat to a student-led movement in a historic election, marking a potential political turning point after more
articles.body: Serbia’s Aleksandar Vučić has conceded defeat to a student-led movement in a historic election, marking a potential political turning point after more than a decade of his dominance. While the choice of the next prime minister remains uncertain, the movement has brought together several prominent Serbian figures, reflecting its growing political influence.The Student List, a political grouping of 250 representatives comprising academics, doctors, engineers, actors and sports personalities, secured a majority in the 250-member parliament, although its diverse political positions could complicate efforts to form a government.The Student List won 2,267,615 votes, or 52.71%, translating into 140 seats. The “Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia” list secured 1,685,022 votes, or 39.17%, winning 104 seats.Who makes up the Student List?Unlike conventional parties, the Student List has no single leader. During nearly two years of protests, students made decisions through closed-door meetings known as “plenums”, avoiding a formal leadership structure they feared could be targeted by the authorities.According to Guardian, at the movement’s headquarters in Belgrade, professor Radomir Saičić said, “Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard. Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future.”According to Radio Free Europe Radio Liberty, among its prominent figures is Dejan Šoškić, a former governor of the National Bank of Serbia, who has called corruption “much more prevalent [in Serbia] than in neighboring countries.” He has pledged investigations into public officials’ property and reforms linked to Serbia’s European Union membership, while criticising Western sanctions against Russia.Ilija Srđanović, a cardiologist and university professor named the list’s lead candidate in September, has said it will prioritise tackling “organized crime and corruption”. He has not ruled out becoming prime minister, saying the grouping has “more than one candidate for every position.”Former basketball star Dejan Bodiroga is another prominent name, although his political positions remain unclear. Other candidates include heritage expert Zivkov, who challenged the government over plans for a Trump-branded hotel at Belgrade’s NATO-damaged General Staff site, and engineer Zoran Djajić, who raised concerns about construction work before the fatal Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse.Farmer Zlatko Kokanović, is a prominent opponent of Rio Tinto’s proposed Jadar lithium and boron mining project. He has pledged to pursue a permanent ban on exploration and extraction, bringing environmental protection into the movement’s political agenda.Playwright Željko Hubač, helped establish the citizens’ group through which the movement contested the election, while actor Tihomir Stanić, ranked eighth, publicly backed its campaign. Other candidates include Mirjana Nikolić, rector of the University of Arts in Belgrade; civil engineering academic Sanja Frić; geological engineer Zoran Đajić; and lawyer Sarah El Sarag, reflecting the list’s diverse professional backgrounds.How will the new parliament differ?The Student List spans pro-European liberals and Kremlin-friendly nationalists, leaving its policy direction uncertain. Its victory follows protests triggered by the November 2024 station collapse, which killed 16 people and fuelled allegations of corruption and poor construction oversight.Pollsters and the election commission ​put turnout close to 70 per cent, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.The movement must now agree on a prime minister and cabinet, reconcile differences over Europe and Russia, and deliver on demands for accountability.You use AI every day. articles.title: Israel elections: Arab parties could hold key as Netanyahu and Eisenkot set to fall short of victory
articles.summary: The two main blocs appear to have too few seats to form the next government without reliance on Arab parties.
articles.body:
With results still trickling in, it currently appears that Israel's veteran Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done better than was widely predicted with his Likud emerging as the largest single party.

His existing bloc with ultra-nationalist and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties appear to be just short of a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat parliament. However, analysts caution that this is subject to change because the early count was skewed towards areas known to have strong right-wing support.

A dramatic deadlock had been widely forecast as Israelis surged to the polls – with turnout reaching more than 77%.

In Israel's fragmented political system, the signs are that Netanyahu's main rival, the former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, would struggle to command a parliamentary majority without parties led by Israel's Arab minority. According to partial results, they have equalled or gained on their previous record number of seats.

On the campaign trail, most Jewish opposition parties pledged not to work with Arab-majority lists, citing a lack of shared values.

However, Israel's Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers if others were prepared to join forces with them. In this election, Arab Israelis – who often identify as Palestinian citizens of Israel and represent one-fifth of the population – appeared to turn out in unprecedented numbers.

Israeli exit polls suggest no clear winner with Eisenkot's bloc neck and neck with Netanyahu

Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global

Many saw this as a make-or-break election to defeat Israel's most right-wing-ever government, accusing it of stoking racism and hatred.

A huge caveat in all of the current analysis is that the high number of as-yet-uncounted absentee ballots – mostly representing the votes of Israeli soldiers – mean that we are not expecting to have a clear idea of the final results for another day or two.

Overnight, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot addressed their supporters, pledging to form the next government.

"The right-wing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public, among the Jewish public and all those who support the Jewish state. That is what has become clear. A decisive majority," the PM told his celebrating supporters – although he stopped short of declaring victory.

"We must form a strong, national, right-wing government. That is what must be done," he added.

"The public has chosen change," Eisenkot told his Yashar party after exit polls came out – most of which were initially more favourable to the opposition. "The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust. The Israeli public voted against Benjamin Netanyahu continuing as prime minister."

"I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government: stable and good for all of Israeli's citizens. And quickly – because that is what this moment demands, and because the country needs to be brought back together."

There are deep divisions in Israeli society which have been underscored by this and previous elections. They have served not just as referenda on Netanyahu's leadership – as he faces a corruption trial on charges he denies – but also as votes on what kind of country Israel should be.

The PM and his current coalition partners have taken the country on a hardline religious, nationalist trajectory over the past four years. There were mass protests over their plan for a judicial overhaul prior to the unprecedented Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023 which triggered a series of wars – in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

Many Israelis want to see their country more firmly anchored in liberal and secular values.

Remarkably, the past four turbulent years do not appear to have significantly changed voting patterns.

"We see in the polls, that the relative weight of the two main sides: pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu is about the same," Professor Tamar Hermann, a pollster at the Israeli Democracy Institute told me, just prior to the election. "People expected that after October 7th, Netanyahu will be down the drain or even toppled but it didn't happen."

Already, overnight, the main Israeli parties will have begun their intense political wrangling to try to form a new coalition government.

"Each side will try to pull over defectors, or will try to see if they can make a minority government and will try all these different political kinds of wizardry," is how veteran Israeli journalist and author, Yaakov Katz described the process to me. "But it might not work, and it could take weeks or months to see if someone is actually capable of forming a government."

The leaders of the bigger parties typically try to win over smaller ones with promises of cabinet positions, budgets or specific policies.

It is key now to see if those in the main opposition "change bloc" are ready to break a taboo by seeking a political deal with the Arab parties.

On the campaign trail, one of the bloc's leaders, right-wing politician Avigdor Lieberman, went as far as to say that he would not sit in a minority government that relied on their support. It was a sign of the increased mistrust and hostility towards Arab citizens since the 7 October assault.

When I recently met Mansour Abbas, head of Ra'am – the smaller of the two Arab lists – he told me that having been part of the diverse coalition that temporarily unseated Netanyahu between 2021 and 2022, he wanted to join the next government. He believed that potential partners would be more open to an alliance after the election.

"These are familiar and well-known party-political considerations. All politicians in Israel say one thing before elections and speak a different language after elections," he said. "We have experienced this before, and it does not concern us."

Meanwhile, Netanyahu and his allies have already begun an intense campaign of delegitimising the Arab parties – casting their fellow citizens as a threat from within.

After the final results are presented to Israel's largely ceremonial president, Isaac Herzog, next week, he will consult all the leaders of elected parties and ask the candidate who appears most likely to form a coalition to do so.

If that candidate is unable to pull together a majority within a maximum of six weeks, then others could be allowed to try.

If, after all the haggling, no-one is able to form a governing coalition, a new election will be held in the following months, and the entire process will be repeated.

In the meantime, Netanyahu's government stays on in a caretaker role but without the authority to enact major policy changes.

articles.title: In 2019, a Montana rancher found a rare dinosaur skeleton on her land; seven years later, the 70%-complete Nanotyrannus sold for $47.3 million at a New York auction, far above its $9 million top estimate
articles.summary: For decades, the Nanotyrannus occupied an uncertain place in the dinosaur world, caught between scientific classification and the shadow of its much more
articles.body: For decades, the Nanotyrannus occupied an uncertain place in the dinosaur world, caught between scientific classification and the shadow of its much more famous relative, Tyrannosaurus rex. Now, a remarkably preserved skeleton has given the disputed dinosaur a new kind of distinction: becoming one of the most valuable dinosaur fossils ever sold.Known as Jodi, the nearly 70%-complete skeleton fetched $47.3 million at a Sotheby’s auction in New York, dramatically surpassing its top estimate of $9 million. The sale, reported by The Associated Press, makes Jodi the second-most expensive dinosaur fossil ever sold, narrowly behind the $50.1 million record set by a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton called Gus earlier this year.From Montana ranch to Manhattan auctionJodi’s journey began in 2019, when Montana rancher Jodi Pierson discovered the fossil on her property in the Hell Creek Formation, one of North America’s richest and most extensively studied dinosaur sites. The specimen was subsequently excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.According to BBC, the skeleton was initially presented as a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex. That classification reflected a debate that had persisted for decades: whether Nanotyrannus was genuinely a separate dinosaur or simply a younger form of T. rex.Research published last year helped settle the question in favour of Nanotyrannus being a distinct genus. The finding dramatically changed the significance of specimens such as Jodi, placing them among an extremely limited group of known Nanotyrannus skeletons.Jodi is one of only three relatively complete examples known to science. The mounted skeleton stands about 9 feet 6 inches tall and stretches nearly 20 feet from snout to tail.A smaller, sleeker tyrannosaurAlthough Nanotyrannus lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex approximately 67 million years ago, it was considerably smaller. Jodi is roughly half the length of an adult T. rex, while its anatomy gives it a distinctly different appearance.The dinosaur had relatively longer forelimbs, larger hand claws and narrower, blade-like teeth. Its lighter, more slender build has helped distinguish it from the bulkier T. rex.According to CNN, Jodi consists of 191 fossil-bone elements and includes an exceptionally well-preserved skull. The specimen is considered an adult based on its size and bone development. Missing portions have been supplemented with custom 3D-printed and sculpted elements, allowing the skeleton to be displayed in a complete mounted form.Its rarity appears to have been central to the extraordinary auction result. With only a handful of known Nanotyrannus skeletons, the specimen offered collectors an opportunity to own an unusually complete example of a dinosaur whose scientific identity itself was only recently clarified.A fossil with a remarkable neighbourhoodJodi was not the only extraordinary discovery to emerge from the Hell Creek Formation. The same region has produced some of the most important Tyrannosaurus rex fossils ever found.Phipps also discovered the celebrated Dueling Dinosaurs in 2006, roughly eight miles from where Jodi was found. The fossil preserves the remains of a Triceratops and a smaller tyrannosaur apparently locked together, and it later became important to research supporting Nanotyrannus as a distinct genus.Another known Nanotyrannus skeleton, Jane, is housed at the Burpee Museum of Natural History in Illinois.The history of the region therefore adds another layer to Jodi’s importance. What began as a discovery on a working Montana ranch became part of a much larger scientific story about the diversity of tyrannosaurs during the Late Cretaceous period.Twelve minutes, millions of dollarsAt Sotheby’s, six prospective buyers competed for Jodi during a roughly 12-minute auction. The winning bidder, who participated online or by phone, has chosen to remain anonymous.The final price was more than five times the auction house’s lower estimate and substantially exceeded its $6 million to $9 million expected range. The result placed Jodi just behind Gus in the hierarchy of dinosaur fossil sales. The Stegosaurus known as Apex, which sold for $44.6 million in 2024, now ranks third, states BBC report.The price also highlights the extraordinary market that has developed around scientifically significant fossils, particularly exceptionally preserved dinosaur skeletons, adds CNN.The debate beyond the auction roomJodi’s sale has also revived a long-running debate over who should own important fossils and where they should ultimately be kept.Scientists have expressed concern that privately owned specimens can disappear from public view, limiting opportunities for researchers to study them and preventing museums, students and visitors from accessing them.BBC reported that palaeontologists have warned that increasingly high auction prices could encourage a new era of fossil collecting among ultra-wealthy buyers. The concern is particularly acute for rare specimens whose scientific importance may not yet be fully understood.At the same time, the debate is not entirely one-sided. The excavation of large fossils can require considerable expertise, labour, equipment and financial investment, particularly when specimens are located on privately owned land.For now, Jodi’s future remains uncertain. Its anonymous new owner has acquired a fossil that is not only exceptionally rare but also scientifically significant at a moment when Nanotyrannus has finally emerged from decades of classification controversy.Whether Jodi becomes part of a public exhibition or disappears into a private collection, its extraordinary sale has ensured that this once-mysterious dinosaur will remain at the centre of the palaeontology conversation.Images Courtesy: ReutersYou use AI every day. articles.title: 74-year-old Florida man charged with murder offers to plead guilty for a Philly cheesesteak, fries and Pepsi, saying he'll accept life in prison; judge rejects his bizarre deal
articles.summary: A 74-year-old Florida man facing a first-degree murder charge offered to plead guilty and accept a life sentence if a judge agreed to give him a Philly
articles.body: A 74-year-old Florida man facing a first-degree murder charge offered to plead guilty and accept a life sentence if a judge agreed to give him a Philly cheesesteak, fries and a Pepsi. Robert Kessler made the unusual proposal on October 26, 2026, during jury selection in his trial over the 2021 death of 47-year-old Stephanie Crone-Overholt. He also argued that accepting the deal would save taxpayers the expense of a trial. However, Hillsborough Circuit Judge Nick Nazaretian rejected the request, explaining that he could not provide food as an incentive for a guilty plea. Kessler subsequently withdrew his offer and asked the court to proceed with jury selection. He faces charges of first-degree murder and abuse of a dead body.Florida man specifies his demands for a guilty pleaKessler made the offer after Judge Nazaretian explained that he could enter an open guilty plea, potentially receive a life sentence and bring the case to an end without a trial.In response, Kessler told the court he would accept the arrangement in exchange for a Philly cheesesteak, an order of fries and a Pepsi.When the judge asked him to clarify his request, Kessler specified that he wanted onions and mayonnaise on his sandwich, along with fries and a 20-ounce soft drink.He argued that the arrangement would benefit taxpayers by avoiding the cost of a lengthy criminal trial. However, the judge made it clear that a guilty plea could not be exchanged for a meal.“I can't obviously give food to people to enter a plea,” Nazaretian said, describing the proposed arrangement as inappropriate.The judge offered to ensure that Kessler received lunch that day but did not promise him the specific meal he had requested.Why the judge rejected the offerThe judge's response meant that Kessler could not secure the proposed arrangement. A guilty plea must be entered through the proper legal process, rather than in exchange for a personal reward from the court.After the judge rejected his request, Kessler indicated that he did not want to proceed with the proposed plea and asked for jury selection to continue.He suggested that he might have considered pleading guilty if he had received the sandwich, but acknowledged that the judge was unlikely to agree.Consequently, the exchange did not result in a guilty plea, and the criminal proceedings continued.Who is Robert Kessler?Kessler is accused of killing Stephanie Crone-Overholt, a 47-year-old woman originally from Pennsylvania, and disposing of her dismembered remains in McKay Bay near Tampa.He faces charges of first-degree murder and abuse of a dead body. If convicted of first-degree murder, he faces a mandatory life sentence, according to reports on the case.Kessler has been in custody since 2021 and has been awaiting trial for nearly five years. He initially chose to represent himself despite having no formal legal training and facing significant challenges because of his visual impairment.The judge repeatedly warned him about the risks of defending himself in a serious criminal case. His decision to represent himself became a major issue during the proceedings.What happened to Stephanie Crone-Overholt?Crone-Overholt's dismembered remains were discovered by fishermen in McKay Bay in November 2021, prompting a criminal investigation.According to allegations outlined in an investigative affidavit, she had been staying at a home shared by Kessler and his daughter shortly before she disappeared.The affidavit also described an alleged argument between Kessler and Crone-Overholt. Kessler's daughter reportedly told investigators that Crone-Overholt had asked for $200 so she could leave.Investigators allege that Kessler killed the woman and disposed of her remains in the bay. He has been charged in connection with her death, but the allegations must be established through the criminal proceedings.Evidence cited by investigatorsThe prosecution's case includes witness accounts and forensic evidence gathered during the investigation.According to reports describing the affidavit, at least three witnesses told investigators they had seen a man matching Kessler's description throwing bags into the bay around the time of Crone-Overholt's disappearance.Investigators also reportedly found blood evidence in Kessler's home and vehicles that testing linked to Crone-Overholt.The prosecution is expected to rely on such evidence as it presents its case. The defence has challenged aspects of the evidence, including a witness identification.Kessler's guilt or innocence will ultimately be determined through the legal process. He remains accused of the offences and is presumed innocent unless convicted.Kessler changes his mind about representing himselfThe cheesesteak proposal was not the only unusual development during the trial proceedings.Kessler initially insisted on representing himself, declining the assistance of his public defender despite warnings about the difficulties of handling a murder trial without legal training.His eyesight also presented practical challenges. During earlier proceedings, he described his vision as severely limited, saying he could barely distinguish objects. The court discussed ways to help him access documents and participate in his defence.On October 27, Kessler changed his position and indicated that he no longer wanted to represent himself, turning again to his public defender. He also told the judge that he preferred not to remain physically present in the courtroom during the trial.Nazaretian warned that being absent could disadvantage his defence, as Kessler might miss testimony or lose opportunities to alert his lawyer to information relevant to the case. The judge said jurors would be instructed not to interpret his absence as evidence of guilt or innocence.The proceedings continued as the court addressed these issues and moved forward with the murder trial.You use AI every day. articles.title: Wildlife enthusiast spots the critically endangered Burmese big-headed turtle in northern Thailand: The rare encounter amazes viewers and raises concerns about hunting, the pet trade and wildlife protection

articles.body: A turtle with a disproportionately large head, powerful claws and a prehistoric appearance has caught the attention of wildlife lovers after an unexpectedly rare encounter in northern Thailand. During an expedition with @exploreherpetology, a wildlife enthusiast spotted the Burmese big-headed turtle (Platysternon peguense), describing the sighting as a dream come true. The excitement was unmistakable, but the encounter also drew attention to the threats facing this reptile.A rare encounter that almost seemed impossibleThe video captures the enthusiast's disbelief at finding the turtle. “No way is it there?” the person exclaims before celebrating the discovery.According to the account shared alongside the footage, the group had heard that the turtle was spotted earlier, but it had already been released. The chance of seeing it again seemed slim. Finding it still there turned an uncertain moment into an extraordinary wildlife encounter.The enthusiast called it one of their “literal dream animals”, revealing how meaningful the sighting was to someone who had hoped to see the species for years.What makes the Burmese big-headed turtle so unusual?Its appearance makes the turtle difficult to mistake for an ordinary pond turtle. Its large head, long tail and strong claws give it a distinctive, almost prehistoric look.The species belongs to the family Platysternidae and is known for its unusually large head, which it cannot fully withdraw into its shell. Its physical features make it especially fascinating to reptile enthusiasts and wildlife researchers.However, its unusual appearance is only one part of its story. The turtle's survival in its natural habitat matters far more than its popularity in photographs.Hunting and the pet trade threaten its survivalThe enthusiast described the Burmese big-headed turtle as critically endangered and highlighted hunting for the pet trade as a major threat. The video also mentions that turtles are eaten in some mountain communities.Demand for wild animals as pets can place pressure on already vulnerable populations. Removing animals from the wild can reduce the number available to reproduce, particularly when the species is naturally difficult to find.The exact contribution of each threat needs careful assessment, but the broader concern is clear: rare wildlife cannot withstand unlimited collection and hunting.ID@undefined Caption not available.ID@undefined Caption not available.ID@undefined Caption not available.ID@undefined Caption not available.Social media celebrates the sighting, but raises questionsComments beneath the video ranged from admiration to surprise. Some viewers compared the turtle to a Pokémon or a creature from prehistoric times, while others called it a dream species to encounter in the wild.Not everyone was comfortable with the footage. Several commenters questioned why the animal had been handled, while others urged the group not to reveal its exact location.These concerns highlight an important distinction. Wildlife videos can introduce unfamiliar species to large audiences, but sharing sensitive location details may also make vulnerable animals easier to find and collect. Keeping locations private can be a practical conservation measure.Why a rare sighting should mean more than a viral momentThe encounter is a reminder that some of the world's most remarkable animals remain difficult to see in their natural surroundings. Their rarity should inspire curiosity, but also restraint.Responsible wildlife watching means keeping disturbance to a minimum, avoiding unnecessary handling and leaving animals where they belong. Even well-intentioned encounters can cause stress or expose wildlife to risks.The Burmese big-headed turtle may have captured attention because of its unusual face and prehistoric appearance. articles.title: Karwa Chauth 2026: Why Do Married Women Wait for the Moon to Rise Before Breaking Their Fast?
articles.summary: On Karwa Chauth evening, rooftops across North India fill up with women in red and gold, plates of diyas in hand, all looking in the same direction.
articles.body: On Karwa Chauth evening, rooftops across North India fill up with women in red and gold, plates of diyas in hand, all looking in the same direction. Conversation slows. Someone checks a phone for the moonrise time again. Then a shout goes up from a neighbouring terrace, and everyone turns. The moon is out. For a festival built around fasting and prayer for a husband’s long life, it’s striking how much depends on that one silver circle rising over the buildings. In 2026, Karwa Chauth falls on Thursday, October 29, in India, according to Drik Panchang-based listings, and a day earlier, October 28, for families in the USA and Canada.Why This Particular NightThe name itself tells part of the story. “Karwa” is an earthen pot with a spout. “Chauth” means fourth. The festival falls on the fourth lunar day after the full moon in the month of Kartik.The fast lasts from sunrise to moonrise, and it ends only when the Moon is seen during the Chaturthi tithi. That’s why the date shifts from country to country. The lunar day must be running when the Moon rises in your city.Chaturthi is also closely linked with Lord Ganesha. Many families include Ganesha in the Karwa Chauth puja alongside Shiva and Parvati, asking for obstacles to be removed from married life.The Moon’s Place in the FestivalIn Vedic astrology, the Moon, or Chandra, governs the mind and emotions. It’s also connected with nourishment and longevity. Old texts link it with Soma, the divine nectar of the gods, believed to sustain life.So offering prayers to the Moon for a husband’s long life makes clear sense. The Moon represents emotional bonds and life-giving energy. A woman fasting all day and then greeting the Moon is, symbolically, asking that same energy to protect her marriage.The Moon’s cycle adds meaning too. It waxes and wanes, disappears and returns, month after month. Many see that steady return as a reflection of the hope that a marriage, too, will keep renewing itself through difficult phases.What the Rituals RepresentSargi before dawn. The day starts with a meal prepared by the mother-in-law. It’s a gesture of care and a small bridge between two women connected by one family. In many homes, it matters as much emotionally as it does practically.The karwa. The clay pot, filled with water, sits at the centre of the puja. Water stands for life and continuity. In older village customs, women also exchanged karwas, a way to build friendships among wives who had married into the same area from far away.The katha. The story of Queen Veeravati is told in many homes. Her loving brothers, unable to watch her suffer, tricked her into ending her fast early by showing a false moon made with a lamp behind a tree. Her husband fell gravely ill as a result, and only her renewed devotion restored him. The story underlines the importance of waiting for the real Moon.The sieve. Women look at the Moon through a chalni, then at their husbands through the same sieve. One common interpretation says the sieve filters the Moon’s light, passing its blessings on to the husband. Others link it to the Veeravati story, making sure the Moon being greeted is real.Arghya. Water from the karwa is offered to the Moon, poured slowly while a prayer is said. It’s both an act of gratitude and a request.The first sip. The husband offers his wife water and a bite of food to end the fast. In many families, it’s the day's most tender moment.A Festival That Keeps ChangingKarwa Chauth today looks different from what it did a generation ago. Many husbands now fast alongside their wives. Some unmarried women keep the fast for a future partner. Couples living abroad sometimes break the fast on a video call when one of them is travelling.Health remains important. Women who are pregnant, diabetic or on regular medication are advised to speak with a doctor before attempting a waterless fast. Many choose fruit and milk instead, and the spirit of the day stays the same.Get the latest religion news and spiritual insights. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Agnes Wanjiru: Kenyan family protest hearing delay of ex-British soldier accused of murder
articles.summary: No official reason has been given for postponing next month’s hearing to May 2027, family says.
articles.body:
The family of a Kenyan woman allegedly murdered by a British soldier 14 years ago has expressed outrage after an extradition hearing for the accused was postponed until May 2027.

Relatives of Agnes Wanjiru, whose body was found in a septic tank near a British army training camp in Kenya in 2012, described the delay as "completely unacceptable" and accused authorities of failing to keep them informed.

The hearing for Robert James Purkiss, a former British soldier accused of killing the 21-year-old mother, had been due next month. The family said it had now been postponed until May 2027. Purkiss was arrested in the UK last November and is fighting extradition to Kenya to face trial for murder. He denies the allegation.

Wanjiru's niece, Esther Njoki, told the BBC that the family learnt of the postponement through the UK embassy and had received no official explanation.

"We have exercised patience and endured uncertainty for years, but our patience is now being taken advantage of," she said in a statement.

"Agnes deserves justice. Her daughter Stacy deserves answers about what happened. And as a family, we deserve to be treated with dignity and kept informed about proceedings that profoundly affect our lives."

The family said it had already raised money and made arrangements to travel to the UK for the hearing, which was due to take place in three weeks.

It is now calling on the authorities to expedite the proceedings, warning that the latest postponement means the case will enter its 15th year without a trial.

The family said a UK court is expected next week to give the reasons for the hearing delay.

Wanjiru disappeared in March 2012 after spending an evening at a hotel in Nanyuki, about 200km (124 miles) north of Nairobi, where British soldiers were stationed for training.

Her body was found nearly three months later in a septic tank at the hotel. She had suffered stab wounds to her chest and abdomen and left behind a five-month-old daughter.

A Kenyan inquest concluded in 2019 that she had been unlawfully killed by one or two British soldiers.

In September 2025, a Kenyan High Court issued an arrest warrant for a British national after prosecutors presented evidence they said justified bringing murder charges.

Purkiss' lawyers said he intended to contest extradition to Kenya.

The 38-year-old former soldier appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court in February via video link , where he was further remanded in custody.

Last year, the then British Defence Secretary John Healey met Wanjiru's family during a visit to Kenya and pledged his government's support for efforts to secure justice.

The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.
